newsitem.title: UK: LME copper ambles in low end of range on quiet ker.
newsitem.headline: LME copper ambles in low end of range on quiet ker.

text.p: Copper and other base metal prices drifted lower on Wednesday following a largely uneventful London Metal Exchange (LME) options declaration, traders said.

"Copper is right above the $2,380/85 support area. There's not a lot of volume and if we don't see some fund buying come in, we may see copper lower," a trader said, noting that forward lending was featuring in the market.
Three months copper finished the kerb at $2,390, versus Tuesday's afternoon kerb close of $2,395. Cash to three months backwardation narrowed slightly to $60/$62.
The March options declaration had little effect on prices as March copper had been in between strike levels, traders said.

Early inter-office trading had seen copper stronger above $2,400 on news that Asarco's copper output was curtailed due to flooding in southern Peru. A bout of early buying in aluminium had also helped boost prices.
"But there wasn't any volume at those prices -- it was just being marked up," a trader noted, adding that the Asarco news had been factored into the price.
Aluminium was barely changed and was in store for further consolidation after its recent run-up to $1,700 earlier this week, traders said.
Prices finished at $1,685, down just $1 from Tuesday.
Lead fell sharply following a bout of option-related selling which pushed the price to a low of $686. But it finally settled off that support area, at $691, down $7.

Lead's largest open interest had been on $725 March calls, and the unwinding of cover on those undeclared options pushed prices lower. Chinese selling has also featured heavily in lead's decline from recent highs above $700, traders said.

Narrowing cash/threes backwardation, which had shot up to about $20 earlier in the week on April tightness, suggested the squeeze may be coming to an end as lending emerged. The backwardation was last at $5/$8.
Nickel continued languishing at lower levels after Tuesday's sharp tumble on news regarding labour problems at Russia's Norilsk Nickel complex that suggested a long stoppage was unlikely.
Prices were slightly firmer at $8,150, up $50.
Zinc continued to quietly hang on to most of this week's strong gains in which speculative and producer short covering propelled it to 4-1/2 year highs.
It was last at $1,245, down $5 from Tuesday but above support at $1,240.

"Another good close and prices could now move up to test the $1,270/80 area, where there is a gap on the chart," brokers Brandeis said in a report, adding that Far Eastern selling on highs has capped prices for now.
Tin was little changed at $5,850, down $10, while alloy was last bid at $1,560 compared to Tuesday's $1,555.
